title: Have a good trip
goal: Say goodbye, pass on what other people said, and peek at a Bulgarian feature that almost no other European language has: a verb form showing that you **did not witness** the event yourself.
bekal: saying goodbye and wishing someone a good journey
offering good wishes for different occasions

dialogs.title: Диалог — The day before leaving
dialogs.intro: Maria and Ani meet one last time before Ani goes home. Watch the verb form in the line about Ivan — Maria didn't witness what she is reporting.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes. I can't believe how fast the time has gone.
lines.literal: yes. not — I-can — that — I-believe, that — passed — so — fast.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Of course. I've already bought a ticket for March.
lines.literal: understands — itself. already — I-bought — ticket — for — March.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: Ivan says you spoke only Bulgarian for a whole week.
lines.literal: Ivan — says, that — you-were — spoken(f) — only — in — Bulgarian — whole — week.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: No, he isn't. You've learned a lot.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Thank you for everything. I'll miss you.
lines.literal: thank-you — for — everything. will — to-me — you-be-missing.

lines.speaker: Мария:
lines.id: Me too. Write to me, OK?
lines.literal: also — you — to — me. write — to-me, will-it-do — (question)?

notes: **Че means "that" and is almost never dropped.** *Мисля, че…* (I think that…), *Казва, че…* (he says that…), *Радвам се, че…* (I'm glad that…). ⚠️ English often drops "that"; Bulgarian almost always uses it, and always with a comma before it.

**Че and да must not be mixed up.** *Че* introduces a fact: *Знам, че работиш* (I know you work). *Да* introduces something wanted or not yet real: *Искам да работиш* (I want you to work). Picking the wrong one changes the meaning completely.
**На добър път literally means "to a good road"** and is said to anyone setting off on a journey. Other send-offs: *Лек път!* (have a light journey) and *Успех!* (good luck).

**Ще ми липсваш — "I'll miss you".** Notice the flipped pattern from Unit 17: the subject is **you**, so the verb form is *липсваш*. Literally: "you will be missing to me". ⚠️ Not *ще те липсвам*, which means the opposite.
**Става ли? means "OK? all right?"** and is added to the end of a request to soften it. The answer is *Става!* — OK, deal. It's one of the most versatile words in everyday Bulgarian.
**Пиши ми — "write to me", meaning "keep in touch".** The command form for a friend. In everyday speech, Bulgarians use *пиши ми* for text messages, just like "text me" in English.
**Обещавам means "I promise"** and is one of the regular Group III verbs. Its past form is *обещах*.

**If you've reached this page, you've done something few people do.** Most people who start Bulgarian stop at the alphabet page. Twenty dialogues, more than eight hundred exercise lines and three hundred and fifty words later — you are no longer one of them.

grammars.title: Преизказно наклонение — the form for news you didn't witness
body: This is the most famous Bulgarian feature, and almost no other European language has it. When you report something you **didn't witness yourself** — you heard it from someone, read it in the news, worked it out — the verb form changes.

head: You saw it
You heard it from someone
English
rows: He works in Sofia. / So they say.
Ivan is ill. / Apparently Ivan is ill.

after: This form is used all through Bulgarian news broadcasts, in every fairy tale, and in every conversation about other people. It is not a marker of doubt — it is a marker of **source**. The speaker isn't saying the news is false, only that they didn't witness it.

⚠️ You **don't need to use it** at A1. The safe and perfectly correct way is to name the source openly with *че*: *Иван казва, че тя работи в София.* Everyone will understand, and nobody will think it wrong.
All you need to do now is **recognize it when you hear it** — so you know the speaker is passing on news, not testifying. The full system is waiting for you at A2.

grammars.title: Reporting what others said
body: The simplest and safest way, and enough for all of A1.
after: Notice that the verb in the reported clause **does not shift tense** the way it does in English. *Той каза, че работи* means "he said he was working" — the present is kept even though the main verb is past. Just keep the tense the speaker originally used.

Say it
Occasion

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note that **честит** follows the gender of what is celebrated: *честит рожден ден* (masculine), *честита Нова година* (feminine), *честито дете* (neuter, for the birth of a child). One word, three forms — just like any other adjective.
Cover the right column and check whether you still remember. Wherever you stumble, go back to that unit — one unit, twenty minutes, and it comes back.

blocks.title: One sentence to take home
items: **Не се притеснявай — говори!** (*neh seh pree-tes-nya-VAI — go-VO-ree*) — "Don't be shy, just talk!"

This is the sentence you'll hear most from Bulgarians once they know you're learning their language. They aren't just being polite. Bulgarians rarely meet foreigners who can speak their language, and your first sentence will be remembered all day.

Nobody will laugh at your mistakes. Your effort will be valued more than you expect. And the only way to turn these twenty units into a living language is to take them off this page and into a real conversation — today, not once you feel ready.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
Write the right wish in Bulgarian.
items: Your friend has a birthday. You say ____.
Your friend is about to fly somewhere. You say ____.
Your friend is ill. You say ____.
Your friend just sneezed. You say ____.
Your friend has an exam tomorrow. You say ____.
